analysis.one_liner: Lets wage-theft lawsuits stay alive while federal wage investigations are underway.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 29, 2010 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it died with no hearing or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: When the Department of Labor investigates an employer for unpaid minimum wages or overtime, the investigation can take months or years. Under current law, workers only have a limited window (a statute of limitations) to sue for back pay, and that clock keeps running while the investigation drags on — so by the time it ends, some workers may be barred from suing. This bill would pause that clock from the moment the Labor Department notifies the employer of an investigation until the employer is told the investigation is over.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who were shortchanged on minimum wage or overtime pay. If a federal wage investigation stretches out, they keep their right to sue for the back pay they are owed instead of losing it to an expiring deadline.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers owed unpaid wages or overtime

how_it_helps.text: Pauses the statute of limitations for claims of unpaid minimum wage, unpaid overtime, and related liquidated damages from the date the Labor Department notifies an employer of an investigation until the employer is notified the investigation has concluded.
Adds this tolling rule to Section 6 of the Portal-to-Portal Act, which sets the two-year (three-year for willful violations) time limit for bringing Fair Labor Standards Act wage claims.

Prevents lengthy federal investigations from quietly erasing workers' day in court — the employer is on notice of the potential claim while the government investigates, but the worker's deadline does not run during that time.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have underpaid workers — including restaurants, retail chains, construction firms, and other businesses that rely on hourly labor — would face a longer window during which workers could sue for back pay, plus the liquidated damages the law adds on top.

drawbacks.text: Because investigations can run for a long time, employers would face an open-ended extension of their legal exposure: a single Labor Department inquiry could freeze the deadline for suing indefinitely, which businesses would argue makes wage-and-hour liability harder to plan for or close out.

The bill applies the pause broadly to 'any eventual cause of action' related to the investigation, so even workers who were not the focus of the probe could gain extra time to sue, expanding litigation beyond the employees the government actually looked into.

Employers (especially small ones) would bear the cost of defending older claims and paying back wages plus liquidated damages for periods that would otherwise have been beyond the statute of limitations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real and targeted: it closes a gap where the government's own slow investigation could cost an employee the right to recover wages the employer was found to have withheld. The cost falls on employers, particularly those that underpay, in the form of longer exposure to back-pay suits and doubled damages. The bill is narrow — it does not create new rights or new penalties, only preserves existing ones during investigations — so the main criticism is fairness to employers whose liability clocks would be paused indefinitely, not the size of what workers would recover.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee in late September 2010, and with the Congress ending three months later and no hearing, markup, or floor action, it simply expired there.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey introduced the bill in the Senate on September 29, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress, with Sen. Tom Harkin as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never considered it, and it never came to a Senate vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who owe workers unpaid minimum wage or overtime — and any business facing wage-and-hour claims — are better off, because the extended window for workers to sue never became law. The bill died quietly in committee with only one cosponsor, so no group had to fight it on the floor.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wage Theft Prevention Act in the Senate on September 29, 2010.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 29, 2010 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, so there is no record of how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have extended how long these employers can be sued for unpaid minimum wage and overtime whenever the Labor Department investigates them, adding exposure to back pay plus doubled damages. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran against workers trying to recover wages they were shortchanged.
